nameStory: The striped green sea anemone gets its name from the distinctive orange or yellow stripes that run along its olive-green column, creating a colorful pattern that makes it stand out among New England's marine life. Some folks also call it the orange-striped green sea anemone, which captures both its base color and its eye-catching striped decoration.
description: This small sea anemone looks like a living flower stuck to rocks in the intertidal zone, with a soft, cylindrical body topped by delicate tentacles that wave in the current. The body column is typically olive-green with bright orange or yellow vertical stripes running down its sides. When fully extended, it's usually about an inch tall and wide, though it can scrunch down to a small, jelly-like blob when the tide goes out or when disturbed. Like all sea anemones, it's actually an animal that catches small prey with its stinging tentacles.

idTips.label: Striped column
idTips.description: Look for distinctive orange, yellow, or white vertical stripes running down the olive-green body column - these stripes are your best identifying feature and make this species unmistakable

idTips.label: Size and shape
idTips.description: Small and compact, typically about an inch tall when extended, with a smooth cylindrical column that feels soft and squishy to gentle touch

idTips.label: Tentacles
idTips.description: Numerous translucent tentacles arranged in rings around the mouth, usually pale green or yellowish, that retract quickly when touched

idTips.label: Base attachment
idTips.description: Firmly attached to hard surfaces by a sticky base that grips rocks, shells, or pier pilings - you'll need to gently pry to remove it

idTips.label: Closed appearance
idTips.description: When disturbed or at low tide, contracts into a small dome-shaped blob with the stripes still visible on the wrinkled surface

habitat: Found in the rocky intertidal zone along New England's coast, typically attached to rocks, pier pilings, shells, or other hard surfaces in tide pools or areas that are regularly covered and uncovered by tides. They prefer somewhat protected areas with good water circulation rather than spots that get heavy wave action. You'll often find them in the mid to lower intertidal zone where they won't be out of water for too long.

seasonality.spring: Most active as water temperatures begin to warm, with tentacles fully extended during high tides for feeding. This is when they're easiest to spot and photograph.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period with frequent feeding and reproduction. Tentacles are often extended and the striped patterns are most vibrant.
seasonality.fall: Still active but may be less extended as water temperatures drop. Stripes remain visible even when contracted.
seasonality.winter: Least active but still present, often staying more contracted. Hardy individuals can be found year-round in deeper tide pools that don't freeze.

funFact: This sea anemone is actually an ocean traveler that hitchhiked to New England from Asia, likely arriving on ship hulls or with transported oysters - it's become so well-established here that many people assume it's native, but it's actually one of our most successful marine immigrants!
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with other small sea anemones, but the vertical stripes on the column make this species unmistakable - no other common New England anemone has this distinctive striped pattern. Remember: stripes = lineata (which means 'lined' in Latin).
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'green' sea anemone, the base color can vary from olive-green to brownish-green, and it's the stripes rather than the exact shade of green that matter for identification. This species shows remarkable variation in its appearance, which is why it was described multiple times by early scientists who thought they were looking at different species.
compareHints: The striped green sea anemone is easily distinguished from its relatives by its distinctive vertical stripes - the ghost anemone (Diadumene leucolena) is typically white or pale without prominent stripes. While other Diadumene species may have some markings, none have the bold, contrasting vertical stripes that make lineata so recognizable.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The Ghost Anemone differs from its relative the Striped Green Sea Anemone by lacking the distinctive green coloration and striped pattern of its cousin.
Compared to its relatives, the striped green sea anemone has distinctive green coloration with stripes, while the ghost anemone appears much paler or translucent.
